message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a legal game of chess is astronomically large.  In fact, the best estimates put it at roughly

\[
\boxed{10^{43}\text{–}10^{44}\text{ possible positions}}
\]

This figure comes from extensive combinatorial analysis and computer enumeration of legal board states.  It is often quoted as “the Shannon number” for the size of the chess position space, and it is many orders of magnitude larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe.  (For comparison, the number of possible *games*—i.e., sequences of moves—is estimated at about \(10^{123}\).)

But the number of possible games (sequences of moves) is about 10^123. The number of possible positions (arrangements) is about 10^43. The Shannon number is 10^120 for game tree complexity.
